title: Man. Post. Cap. II: mode-2 propagation; consensus if hereditary corruption truly sin; Rom 5:12; Plac. on Gar.
pass_a_gloss: The same must be said of the second mode: for as truly as Adam's sin is said to have passed into us, to have been derived, transmitted, propagated, so truly also it is said to be imputed to us. But it has been propagated, not as it was a transient act, but as it was a permanent viciousness, not as it was the sin of a person, but as it was the sin of nature, not as it once ceased to be in the nature of things, but as it adheres to human nature, and with it is multiplied and propagated. Further, as my nature propagated and derived from Adam differs in number from Adam's nature, so the sin derived and propagated from Adam differs in number from Adam's sin. Thus far, unless my mind deceives me, there is supreme consensus between us, provided you are unwilling to deny that hereditary corruption is truly a sin imputable to the unregenerate, or rather to be imputed unto condemnation. But if you deny that, this third controversy will arise between me and you, which although it will be able to be finished by proper arguments, yet there will be no need of them: for with the exceptions of Socinus, Pelagius, and Pighius refuted (which I did in the Theses), it is necessary to confess that that universal condemnation which the Apostle inculcates at Rom. 5:12 arises proximately from that corruption alone which flowed from Adam's fall. PLAC. These three last acceptations of Adam's sin D. Gar. agitates in a marvelous manner: with what mind? I know not. For that helps nothing the status of the question, or the cause which he urges, and uselessly delays the Reader. For what does he reprehend in that distinction of the name? Does he charge it with falsity? Not at all. Does he deny that there is consensus in that matter? By no means. What then does he do? Hear him himself.
pass_b_english: The same holds for the second sense: as truly as Adam's sin is said to have passed into us—derived, transmitted, propagated—so truly it is said to be imputed to us. But it was propagated not as a passing act, but as lasting viciousness; not as the sin of a person, but as the sin of nature; not as something that once ceased to exist, but as what clings to human nature and is multiplied and propagated with it. And as my nature, derived from Adam, differs numerically from Adam's nature, so the sin derived and propagated from Adam differs numerically from Adam's sin. Thus far, unless I am mistaken, we are in full agreement—provided you will not deny that hereditary corruption is truly a sin to be imputed to the unregenerate, or rather to be imputed unto condemnation. If you deny that, a third controversy rises between us; and though it could be settled by its own arguments, they will not be needed: once Socinus's, Pelagius's, and Pighius's exceptions are answered (as I did in the Theses), we must admit that the whole condemnation Paul presses in Romans 5:12 arises proximately from that corruption alone which flowed from Adam's fall. Placeus. Master Garissoles works up these three last senses of Adam's sin strangely—to what end I do not know. It helps neither the state of the question nor the cause he urges, and only wastes the reader's time. What fault does he find in the distinction of the name? That it is false? Not at all. That there is no consensus on the point? By no means. What then is he doing? Hear him.
source_text: Idem de secundo modo dicendum: quam enim vere dicitur peccatum Adami in nos transiisse, derivatum, transmissum, propagatum esse, tam vere etiam dicitur nobis imputari. Propagatum est autem, non qua fuit actio transiens, sed qua fuit vitiositas permanens, non qua fuit peccatum personae, sed qua fuit peccatum naturae, non qua olim esse desiit in rerum natura, sed qua naturae humanae adhaeret, cumque ea multiplicatur et propagatur. Porro ut natura mea propagata et derivata ab Adamo differt numero a natura Adami, sic peccatum ab Adamo derivatum et propagatum differt numero a peccato Adami. Hactenus, nisi me fallit animus, inter nos summus est consensus, modo nolis negare corruptionem haereditariam esse vere peccatum irregenitis imputabile, vel potius imputandum ad condemnationem. Quod si id neges, haec tertia exorietur inter me et te controversia, qua quamvis propriis argumentis confici poterit, tamen iis nihil opus erit: nam refutatis (quod feci in Thesibus) exceptionibus Socini, Pelagii, et Pighii, necesse est fateri, universam illam condemnationem, quam Apostolus ad Rom. v.12. inculcat, ex sola illa corruptione, quae a lapsu Adami fluxit, proxime enasci. PLAC. Has tres ultimas peccati Adamici acceptiones D. Gar. mirum in modum exagitat: qua mente? nescio. Nihil enim id juvat statum questionis, aut causam quam agit, et Lectorem inutiliter moratur. Quid enim in ea nominis distinctione reprehendit? Num eam falsitatis arguit? minime. Num negat in ea re consensum esse? nequaquam. Quid ergo agit? ipsum audi.

choices.choice: Propagated as nature's sin; consensus if hereditary corruption truly imputable; else Rom 5:12 from corruption alone
